nodes.label: Strategy Pattern
nodes.rationale: Encapsulates a whole algorithm as a swappable object held via composition; can be swapped at runtime without editing the context class; adding a new algorithm means adding a new class (OCP). More flexible than Template Method.

nodes.label: Template Method Pattern
nodes.rationale: Fixes the order of algorithm steps in one method and lets subclasses override only some steps via inheritance; easier to understand because the order is fixed at compile time, but carries Fragile Base Class / LSP risk if an override breaks the template's invariants.

nodes.label: Head-based Sampling
nodes.rationale: Decides keep/drop at the first span before outcome is known: cheap and fast but can drop rare error or slow traces.

nodes.label: Tail-based Sampling
nodes.rationale: Waits for the whole trace to finish, then keeps 100% of error/slow traces and samples normal ones; costs collector memory for buffering.

nodes.label: Build Once, Deploy Many
nodes.rationale: Build a single artifact once and promote the same bytes through every environment; only config/env vars differ. Rebuilding per environment risks dependency drift and works-on-my-machine failures.

nodes.label: CI/CD Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Assembly line with quality gates (build, unit test, integration test, package, staging, production); failure at a gate stops the change so bugs are caught early where fixes are cheap.

nodes.label: Pipeline Feedback Loop Length

nodes.rationale: Accepted: failure detected within 6s with automatic failover; during that window some requests fail so client retry is added and timeout tuned carefully.

nodes.label: Heartbeat
nodes.rationale: Live node announces itself periodically; missing signals beyond a timeout mean failure. Timeout needs tuning: too short gives false positives, too long slows detection.

nodes.label: Architecture Tactics
nodes.rationale: Small design decisions targeting one specific quality attribute; smaller and more specific than architectural patterns, which are built from many tactics.

nodes.label: Tactics Make Trade-offs Concrete and Testable
nodes.norm_label: tactics make trade-offs concrete and testable
nodes.rationale: Saying 'we chose microservices for availability' is not a decision; naming heartbeat detection in 6s plus spare promotion turns it into an ATAM-style scenario.

nodes.label: Tactics and Patterns Live at Different Layers
nodes.norm_label: tactics and patterns live at different layers
nodes.rationale: A pattern says the big picture; tactics are the actual mechanisms that make it work. One tactic (e.g. heartbeat) can serve many patterns.

nodes.label: Atomic Conditional UPDATE

nodes.community_name: Tragedy of the Commons (CI Runner Pool) (cluster)

nodes.label: Shared Player Retention Metric
nodes.community_name: Tragedy of the Commons (CI Runner Pool) (cluster)

nodes.rationale: Tragedy of the Commons arises when each party sees only its own boundary; Shifting the Burden arises when long-term capability is left outside the decision boundary.

nodes.label: Atomic Operation (Compare-and-Swap / Row Lock)
nodes.rationale: Structure fix making one valve through which all requests queue, so a race cannot occur structurally.

nodes.label: Check-Then-Act Race Condition
nodes.rationale: Server reads that the item exists then writes the award as two separate steps, so concurrent requests can both believe they won; low-ping players win repeatedly.

nodes.label: Increase Server Tick Rate (parameter fix)
nodes.rationale: Shrinks the read-write window but does not change the non-atomic flow shape; only probability changes.

nodes.label: Atomic Stock Reservation at Single Source of Truth
nodes.norm_label: atomic stock reservation at single source of truth
nodes.rationale: Decrement stock atomically in one database before confirming any order; do not decide sales from cache.

nodes.label: Edge Cache Staleness Causing Oversell
nodes.rationale: Edge caches show stock remaining to every node simultaneously while database stock is lower: same read/write separation as boss loot, in e-commerce.

nodes.label: Eventual Consistency for Display, Strong Consistency for Selling
nodes.norm_label: eventual consistency for display, strong consistency for selling
nodes.rationale: Goals/mental-model fix: stock correctness outranks display speed; allow stale display but enforce strong consistency at sale decision.

nodes.label: Retry Amplification at Peak
nodes.rationale: Failed checkouts trigger automatic client retries that add load at the worst moment, an extra R loop.

nodes.label: Monorepo Versioning
nodes.rationale: Monorepo with many packages must choose independent vs fixed versioning; choice depends on how independent the packages really are.

nodes.label: Case: Polyrepo to Monorepo Migration
nodes.rationale: Migrated because symptoms (version drift, cross-repo coordination, CI unable to catch cross-repo integration bugs) match what monorepo solves, not because monorepo is always better.

nodes.label: Coupling
nodes.rationale: Measures how much one module knows about another's details.

nodes.label: Decorator Pattern
nodes.rationale: Adds behavior in stackable layers over the same interface, a concrete form of composition over inheritance.

nodes.label: Decorator vs Proxy: Intent Differs
nodes.rationale: Structure is identical; Decorator adds capability while Proxy controls access.

nodes.label: Proxy Pattern
nodes.rationale: Controls access to the real object (lazy loading, access control, caching, remote) without adding behavior.

nodes.label: Event-Driven Architecture (pub-sub, message queue, event bus)
nodes.norm_label: event-driven architecture (pub-sub, message queue, event bus)

nodes.label: Memory Leak from Forgotten Unsubscribe
nodes.rationale: A destroyed observer still referenced by the Subject's list cannot be garbage-collected; most common Observer pitfall, fixed by unsubscribing on unmount/destroy via lifecycle hooks. Second pitfall: non-deterministic notification order.

nodes.label: Observer Pattern
nodes.rationale: Subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them on state change without knowing their concrete types; adding a new observer needs only subscribe(), not editing the Subject (OCP, low coupling). Foundation of event-driven systems.

nodes.label: Shotgun Surgery (scattered VehicleType checks)
nodes.rationale: Scattering if/switch on VehicleType across code is a Shotgun Surgery smell; centralize size-fit logic in a single canFit() on ParkingSpot.

nodes.label: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
nodes.rationale: ParkingSpot knows only its occupancy, Ticket only parking data, ParkingLot finds spots and issues tickets; each has one reason to change.

nodes.label: Disaster Recovery Readiness Levels
nodes.rationale: Lower RTO/RPO costs non-linearly more; choose the level matching tolerable business loss, not always the best.

nodes.label: Layered Problem: Business Logic Coupled to Infrastructure
nodes.norm_label: layered problem: business logic coupled to infrastructure

nodes.label: ADR: Hexagonal Architecture for Core Billing Engine
nodes.norm_label: adr: hexagonal architecture for core billing engine
nodes.rationale: Complex billing rules need fast unit tests and multiple payment gateways later; ports for gateway and repository with gateway adapters, at the cost of upfront interface design.

nodes.label: ADR-004: Use 4+1 as Design Doc Template
nodes.norm_label: adr-004: use 4+1 as design doc template
nodes.rationale: Single-viewpoint design docs missed deployment and runtime concurrency issues until production; require all four views plus key scenarios.

nodes.label: Not Every Project Needs All Five Views
nodes.norm_label: not every project needs all five views
nodes.rationale: Small teams usually need only Logical and Physical; Process View is drawn only when concurrency is genuinely complex.

nodes.label: Cross-Context Integration via API / Event (no shared tables)
nodes.norm_label: cross-context integration via api / event (no shared tables)

nodes.norm_label: sales context (product = price, promotion, publish state)

nodes.norm_label: single shared domain model (breaks at scale)

nodes.label: ADR: Split Product Model into Bounded Contexts by Department
nodes.norm_label: adr: split product model into bounded contexts by department
nodes.rationale: A shared products table caused cross-department regressions and conflicting meanings of 'product status'; separate models per context, connected via API/event, at the cost of cross-context consistency work.

nodes.label: ADR: Waiting Room + Strict Row Lock for Flash Sale
nodes.norm_label: adr: waiting room + strict row lock for flash sale
nodes.rationale: Accepted because business driver #1 is zero overselling; accepts longer waits and extra complexity over optimistic locking risk during retry storms.

nodes.label: Distributed Lock via Redis per Seat
nodes.norm_label: distributed lock via redis per seat

nodes.label: High-Cardinality Data
nodes.rationale: Fields with many unique values (user_id, request_id) enable slicing raw events by many dimensions to find unexpected patterns.

nodes.label: Observability
nodes.rationale: Lets you ask new questions during investigation via ad-hoc queries over raw high-cardinality events; having logs/metrics/traces alone does not make a system observable.

nodes.label: Cardinality Explosion
nodes.rationale: High-cardinality labels create one series per unique value; Prometheus indexes all series in memory so memory balloons until OOM. Logs/traces tolerate high cardinality; metrics do not.

nodes.label: Recording Rule
nodes.rationale: Precompute heavy or frequent queries periodically into a small new metric so dashboards read cheap results; reduces query load but does not fix high-cardinality storage cost.

nodes.label: Case: Hotfix Under GitFlow
nodes.rationale: Process, not the 5-line fix, was the bottleneck: GitFlow is for paced releases and multi-version maintenance; a single-version deployer should use trunk-based or GitHub Flow.

nodes.label: Trunk-Based Development
nodes.rationale: Short-lived branches merged to trunk often with feature flags; no develop branch to sync, hotfix goes straight to main.

nodes.label: Composition
nodes.rationale: Behavior is an injected object swappable at runtime, giving looser coupling than compile-time inheritance.

nodes.label: Favor Composition Over Inheritance
nodes.rationale: Inheritance is the tightest coupling (compile-time, affects all subclasses), conflicting with low coupling; use it only when is-a is always true.

nodes.label: Wrong Dependency Direction Between Layers
nodes.rationale: Business layer imports a concrete data access class, so swapping MySQL for PostgreSQL or unit-testing without a real DB requires editing business code; the problem is unenforced dependency direction, not the layering itself.

nodes.label: Layered Architecture
nodes.rationale: Splits code into Presentation, Business and Data Access layers, each calling only downward; looks tidy but does not enforce dependency direction, so business logic can still bind to concrete infrastructure.

nodes.label: Feature-Based Folder Structure
nodes.rationale: Groups all layers of one feature together (high cohesion); fits growing multi-team systems, at the cost of a harder system-wide overview.

nodes.label: Layer-Based Folder Structure
nodes.rationale: Folders mirror Clean Architecture layers; gives overview of all use cases but one feature change spans many folders (Shotgun-Surgery-like symptom).

nodes.label: The Dependency Rule
nodes.rationale: Source-code dependencies may only point inward toward the center; DIP applied systematically across the whole architecture rather than one class pair. Solves the testability and swappable-infrastructure questions that traditional layering could not.

nodes.label: Framework Leakage into Inner Circles
nodes.rationale: Most common Dependency Rule violation: importing framework types (e.g. Express.Request) into Entities/Use Cases, which forces use-case edits when swapping frameworks.

nodes.label: GitOps
nodes.rationale: Git repo is the single source of truth for desired state; an in-cluster agent pulls and reconciles continuously, so CI never needs credentials into the cluster and every change is in git history.

nodes.label: Pull-based Smaller Attack Surface
nodes.rationale: Push-based requires external CI to hold cluster credentials (compromised pipeline means cluster access); pull-based agent lives inside the cluster so no external credential is distributed.

nodes.label: Infrastructure Drift
nodes.rationale: Real infrastructure diverges from IaC files; plain IaC only reports it and a human chooses to import or re-apply, unlike GitOps which auto-reverts.

nodes.label: Manual Cluster Edit Reverted by Reconciler
nodes.norm_label: manual cluster edit reverted by reconciler
nodes.rationale: kubectl edits made outside Git vanish because the reconciler enforces Git; correct fix, even in an incident, is to commit to Git.

nodes.label: Reconcile Loop
nodes.rationale: Endless loop reads desired state from Git, reads actual state from cluster, applies diff; self-heals drift, so manual cluster edits are reverted on the next cycle.

nodes.label: Plan then Apply Workflow
nodes.rationale: Human reviews the plan diff before apply because some infra changes (e.g. destroy and recreate a database) are irreversible; declarative does not guarantee a safe diff.

nodes.label: Config Drift of Pet Servers
nodes.rationale: Accumulated manual patches over months make a server unreproducible; config management reduces but does not eliminate this because it still mutates the same machine.

nodes.label: Declarative IaC
nodes.rationale: Write the desired end state; the tool diffs against reality and decides what to create/change/delete. Dominant style today.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
nodes.rationale: Describe servers, networks and databases as code (a blueprint) instead of clicking in a cloud console.

nodes.label: ADR: Order Aggregate Excludes Customer Object
nodes.norm_label: adr: order aggregate excludes customer object
nodes.rationale: Accepted: write Order and edit Customer concurrently without collision, at the cost of extra queries when a screen needs both.

nodes.label: Aggregate
nodes.rationale: A cluster of entities and value objects that must change together to protect invariants; the unit that commits or rolls back in one transaction.

nodes.label: Aggregate Root
nodes.rationale: Single entry point allowed to modify anything inside the aggregate; knows how to recompute totals and enforce limits.

nodes.label: Eventual Consistency Between Aggregates
nodes.rationale: Each aggregate is strongly consistent internally; cross-aggregate updates (e.g. VIP upgrade) propagate via events after commit.

nodes.label: StockItem Aggregate
nodes.rationale: Guards the key invariant reserved <= available; if it breaks the system oversells.

nodes.label: Keep Aggregates Small
nodes.rationale: Smaller aggregates mean shorter locks and less contention; larger ones read everything in one place but block concurrent writes.

nodes.label: Reference Other Aggregates by ID Only
nodes.norm_label: reference other aggregates by id only
nodes.rationale: Holding a whole Customer inside Order entangles transactions (locking) and leaves stale data; store customerId only so aggregates stay independent and scalable.

nodes.label: Transactional Boundary
nodes.rationale: One transaction per aggregate; avoids partial saves where Order is stored but some OrderLineItems fail.

nodes.label: Key Hierarchy / Envelope Encryption
nodes.rationale: Master key encrypts data keys so the master can rotate without re-encrypting all data at once.

nodes.label: Blast Radius Control
nodes.rationale: Start experiments in staging or the smallest-impact slice of production, expand gradually only after confidence.

nodes.label: Chaos Engineering
nodes.rationale: Deliberately inject failure in a controlled environment with people ready, rather than let it strike unexpectedly at the worst time (night, peak traffic); proves redundancy/failover really works.

nodes.label: Encryption Key Leak Blast Radius
nodes.rationale: One key for everything means system-wide damage; per-service/tenant keys and fast rotation limit it.

nodes.label: Quorum-approved Failover
nodes.rationale: Promote a new leader only after majority confirmation, because 'I cannot see the primary' is not the same as 'the primary is dead'. Trade-off: slower failover (cross-DC latency) vs preventing split-brain; waiting on a quorum is more accurate than waiting on elapsed time.

nodes.label: Safety Floor in Operational Tooling
nodes.rationale: Humans always mistype, so the tool itself must reject commands that would drop a subsystem below a minimum safe capacity. A plain confirmation prompt is not enough because a mistyper confirms wrongly; a logic check against real system state catches it.

nodes.label: Config Changes Need Canary Too
nodes.rationale: Canary protects against any behavior-changing change (security rules, feature flags, tuning values), not only code bugs. Skipping canary for 'must take effect immediately' security config carries its own risk; speed of protection is not worth an unstoppable global failure.

nodes.label: Regex Complexity Analysis / Worst-case Input Testing
nodes.norm_label: regex complexity analysis / worst-case input testing

nodes.label: ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method)
nodes.rationale: Structured method from the SEI to reason about trade-offs via business drivers, approaches, quality attribute scenarios, analysis, and sensitivity/tradeoff points rather than gut feeling; note condenses the full 9-step method to 5.

nodes.label: Tradeoff Point
nodes.rationale: A decision that affects multiple quality attributes at once (e.g. stricter locking raises consistency but lowers availability); not a design flaw but the nature of the problem.

nodes.label: Fix Structure Not Numbers
nodes.rationale: Effective cures reduce delay or add randomness/dispersion; tuning parameters back and forth often worsens oscillation.

nodes.label: Leverage Point
nodes.rationale: A point in a system where a small change produces a large change in overall behavior; higher leverage means harder and more resisted change.

nodes.label: System Boundary
nodes.rationale: Boundaries are chosen, not given; wider boundaries reveal higher-leverage fixes but exceed one team's authority, while too wide is unanalyzable. Ask whether the boundary is wide enough to see the key feedback loop.

nodes.label: Systems Thinking Unified Toolkit (Case Studies Wrap-up)
nodes.norm_label: systems thinking unified toolkit (case studies wrap-up)
nodes.rationale: Stock/flow shows what accumulates, feedback loops show growth/decay, delays explain late awareness, archetypes name recurring patterns, leverage points say where to act, the iceberg says dig deeper than events.

nodes.label: Emergence (Bot Farm Economy)
nodes.rationale: Properties arising from interactions across thousands of individually valid transactions (shared IPs, systematic timing, wealth concentration), invisible per transaction.

nodes.label: Graph-Based Fraud Detection
nodes.rationale: Structure fix widening the detection boundary from single transactions to relationships between account groups.

nodes.label: Case: Bot Farm Emergent Economy Collapse
nodes.norm_label: case: bot farm emergent economy collapse

nodes.label: Belief: Valid Transactions Mean a Safe System
nodes.norm_label: belief: valid transactions mean a safe system
nodes.rationale: Overlooks emergence; the analysis boundary (single transaction) is too narrow to see the failing system (whole economy) - the boundary problem in disguise.

nodes.label: Parameters/Constants (Level 12)
nodes.rationale: Weakest leverage point (timeout, retry count); most commonly chosen because it is easy, fast and needs no approval.

nodes.label: Alert Threshold Tuning (failed parameter fix)
nodes.rationale: Raising thresholds filtered out important alerts and left the real problem (too few people for the workload) untouched.

nodes.label: Iceberg Level 1: Events
nodes.rationale: What happens right now; reactive firefighting, fix lasts only that day.

nodes.label: Fixes That Fail
nodes.rationale: A fix treats the symptom while the underlying driver persists, so the system drifts back.

nodes.label: Top-Down Architecture Announcement (failed fix)
nodes.rationale: Declaring microservices without changing team structure is parameter-level; the R loop pulls code back and the new architecture becomes renamed folders.

nodes.label: Re-engagement Events (temporary fix)
nodes.rationale: Events bring players back briefly but queue stays bad so they leave again; Fixes That Fail.

nodes.label: Parameter-Tweaking Trap
nodes.rationale: Organizations keep tuning parameters because it is easiest and needs no approval, even though it has least leverage; higher levels need senior authority and meet resistance.

nodes.label: Systems Archetype
nodes.rationale: Recurring named structural patterns that let teams recognize and communicate dynamics without redrawing them.

nodes.label: Fixes That Fail
nodes.rationale: A fast B loop relieves the symptom while a slow R loop builds side effects that eventually make the problem worse than before.

nodes.label: Escalation
nodes.rationale: One large R loop alternating between two parties, each reacting reasonably to the other, ratchets far beyond anyone's intent.

nodes.label: Platform vs Feature Team Quota and Shadow Infra Case
nodes.norm_label: platform vs feature team quota and shadow infra case

nodes.label: Symptom vs Root Cause Detection Question
nodes.norm_label: symptom vs root cause detection question
nodes.rationale: Ask whether the fix addresses the root cause or merely suppresses the symptom, and what is accumulating behind it.

nodes.label: Visible Private Gain vs Diffuse Shared Cost
nodes.norm_label: visible private gain vs diffuse shared cost
nodes.rationale: Gains are clear and fully owned while costs are spread thin across everyone, so each party sees stronger incentive to use more.

nodes.label: Fairness Illusion
nodes.rationale: Rewarding good performance looks fair at every step, yet cumulatively amplifies a small early edge into near-permanent inequality.

nodes.label: Each Step Looks Reasonable Trap
nodes.rationale: Every individual move seems sensible; only the whole trajectory reveals the escalation, which parties inside the loop rarely see.

nodes.label: Independent Optimization
nodes.rationale: Each side only improves its own metric and never looks at the other, unknowingly pushing negative side effects onto it.

nodes.label: System Boundary Too Narrow
nodes.rationale: Each team draws its boundary around itself and cannot see effects exported outside it (recurs from the System Traps module).

nodes.label: Slow Service Example (narrow / medium / wide boundary)
nodes.norm_label: slow service example (narrow / medium / wide boundary)
nodes.rationale: Same latency problem yields code optimization at narrow scope, circuit breakers at medium scope, and company headcount policy at wide scope.

nodes.label: Personal Loot Instancing
nodes.rationale: Goals/mental-model fix: each participant gets an independent item, replacing one contested stock with 1000 independent stocks so no scarcity exists.

nodes.label: Success to the Successful
nodes.rationale: Archetype where the advantaged repeatedly win a shared limited resource; here hidden inside a technical bug favouring low-ping players.

nodes.label: Separate Boss Instance per Guild
nodes.rationale: Goals fix: remove the shared resource so no first action can ignite the loop; same principle as personal loot instancing.

nodes.label: Escalation
nodes.rationale: R loop with no negative links: each side retaliates harder out of belief that not escalating looks weak; here a purely social system with no code to fix.

nodes.label: Game Master Mediation (shared trajectory view)
nodes.rationale: Structure fix: GM sees the whole trajectory and negotiates agreed terms such as split spawn times, cutting the action->feeling-wronged links.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.rationale: Answers questions known in advance via fixed dashboards and alerts (like an annual health checkup).

nodes.label: APM (Application Performance Monitoring)
nodes.rationale: Server-side view of how fast the server responds.

nodes.label: RUM (Real User Monitoring)
nodes.rationale: Collects data from real users' browsers/apps; broad coverage but reactive since a real user must hit the problem first.

nodes.label: Synthetic Monitoring
nodes.rationale: Scheduled simulated requests (mystery shopper) run even with no real users, so problems are found proactively before users hit them.

nodes.label: Pre-aggregated Metric Limitation
nodes.rationale: Aggregated metrics (e.g. per-minute averages) discard dimensions, so unexpected causes (e.g. country=TH, app 2.3.1, iOS only) cannot be sliced out.

nodes.label: APM Client-side Blind Spot
nodes.rationale: Server may respond fast while users still see slowness from large JS bundles, third-party scripts or their own network; only RUM sees this.

nodes.label: Grafana
nodes.rationale: Pure visualization layer, stores no data; each panel picks a data source and queries in that source's language.

nodes.label: Grafana Template Variables
nodes.rationale: One dashboard parameterized by $service dropdown (query, custom, interval variables) replaces dozens of per-service dashboards, avoiding editing 50 copies for each layout change.

nodes.label: Multi-Data-Source Dashboard
nodes.rationale: Combine metric panel (Prometheus) and log panel (Loki) on the same time range so symptom and detail are visible on one screen without switching apps.

nodes.label: Separate Visualization from Storage
nodes.rationale: Same benefit as OpenTelemetry separating API from backend: switching storage (e.g. Elasticsearch to Loki) only changes the data source connection, not the whole dashboard structure.

nodes.label: Blameless Postmortem
nodes.rationale: Ask which system/process allowed the mistake, not who erred; blame culture makes people hide errors and conceal the true root cause.

nodes.label: Postmortem Flow (Timeline, Root Cause, Action Items)
nodes.norm_label: postmortem flow (timeline, root cause, action items)

nodes.label: Toil
nodes.rationale: Repetitive manual work with no lasting value; if it exceeds ~50% of team time the team is permanently firefighting, so automate it before taking new work.

nodes.label: Constructive Feedback Culture
nodes.rationale: Critique the code not the person; explain reasons, suggest fixes, separate opinion from blocker.

nodes.label: Escalation Policy
nodes.rationale: Primary -> Secondary -> Engineering Manager with timeouts (e.g. 5 min) so a critical alert is never left unattended if the primary cannot respond.

nodes.label: Monitor the Monitor
nodes.rationale: Observability needs independent backup layers so a Prometheus failure does not silence the alerts that depend on it.

nodes.label: Monitoring as Single Point of Failure
nodes.norm_label: monitoring as single point of failure
nodes.rationale: Prometheus dying silenced every alert that depends on it; nobody was notified and the failure was noticed by chance.

nodes.label: Silent Email Delivery Failure Incident
nodes.rationale: About 4% of order-confirmation emails failed for weeks with no alert; discovered via support tickets.

nodes.label: Measure-What-Is-Easy Trap
nodes.rationale: Teams new to observability measure HTTP status, CPU, memory because they are easy rather than what users care about.

nodes.label: Complete Toolset Is Not Observability
nodes.rationale: Having metric, log, trace, dashboard, and alert does not guarantee visibility if what is measured is mis-aimed (CCTV pointed the wrong way).

nodes.label: SLI Must Reflect User-Experienced Outcome
nodes.rationale: Ask what the user actually expects from the system, then find the metric reflecting it, even if harder to measure (delivery webhook rather than HTTP response).

nodes.label: Branch Protection (Require review from Code Owners)
nodes.norm_label: branch protection (require review from code owners)

nodes.label: CODEOWNERS
nodes.rationale: Maps paths to owners and auto-requests them as required reviewers; solves who should review, not whether they have time or review deeply.

nodes.label: Last Matching Rule Wins
nodes.rationale: CODEOWNERS like .gitignore uses the last matching rule; putting * at the bottom silently overrides everything with no error.

nodes.label: Human Code Review for Commit Content Quality
nodes.norm_label: human code review for commit content quality

nodes.label: commitlint Checks Format Not Content
nodes.rationale: commitlint validates format only; a meaningless message like 'fix bug' passes, so human review is still needed.

nodes.label: Automation Trusts Human Input Without Semantic Check
nodes.norm_label: automation trusts human input without semantic check
nodes.rationale: commitlint checks format only and semantic-release believes the prefix 100%, so no stage checks whether a change should be breaking.

nodes.label: Command Pattern
nodes.rationale: Wraps a method call as an object with execute() and undo(), enabling queuing, logging (audit trail) and undo/redo instead of direct calls.

nodes.label: State Pattern
nodes.rationale: Moves per-state behavior into separate state classes, removing scattered if-else state checks; each state object knows its own next state, which is what distinguishes it from plain Strategy.

nodes.label: Command undo() Needs Prior State
nodes.rationale: Correct undo requires storing the previous state (e.g. deleted value and its original index), not just calling the opposite method; gets harder when a command affects several objects.

nodes.label: Compose Patterns per Problem Dimension
nodes.rationale: Real systems have separate dimensions (state-dependent behavior, queued requests, swappable algorithm); choosing State, Command and Strategy per dimension and connecting via clear interfaces is the real LLD skill, not memorizing pattern-to-problem mappings.

nodes.label: Canary Cohort Not Representative
nodes.rationale: The first 5% of users may not represent all users (e.g. only new browsers); sample across region and device type instead of simple first-come requests.

nodes.label: Layered Release Safety (pipeline + canary + feature flag)
nodes.norm_label: layered release safety (pipeline + canary + feature flag)
nodes.rationale: Blue-green, canary and feature flags are used together, not exclusively: single artifact via pipeline, canary traffic rollout, then business-logic visibility via flags.

nodes.label: Deploy vs Release
nodes.rationale: Getting code onto production (deploy) is separable from exposing it to users (release); feature flags let teams deploy silently and release gradually without redeploying.

nodes.label: Config Management at Image Build Time
nodes.norm_label: config management at image build time
nodes.rationale: Same tool (Ansible) works either way; the snowflake problem is whether running instances are edited, not the tool. Use config management to build clean images, then never modify running instances.

nodes.label: Immutable Infrastructure
nodes.rationale: Build a new image per change, create new instances, destroy old ones, never SSH-patch; gives easy rollback and cross-environment consistency.

nodes.label: Pets vs Cattle
nodes.rationale: Pets are individually tended mutable servers that are hard to recover; cattle are interchangeable instances built from one image and replaced rather than repaired.

nodes.label: ADR: Event-Driven + Serverless FaaS for Notifications
nodes.norm_label: adr: event-driven + serverless faas for notifications
nodes.rationale: Accepted: decouples sources from channels and is cheap at low traffic, accepting cold-start latency and eventual consistency.

nodes.label: ADR: Containers Over Bare-metal Deployment
nodes.rationale: Accepted: removes env mismatch and speeds deploy; cost is learning Docker and planning registry plus image scanning.

nodes.label: Container
nodes.rationale: An isolated process sharing the host kernel, not a mini VM; lighter and faster than a VM but isolation is weaker.

nodes.label: ADR: Adopt Kubernetes
nodes.rationale: Accepted at 25 microservices: self-healing and scaling, at the cost of learning curve and dedicated cluster care.

nodes.label: Container Orchestration
nodes.rationale: Central system that schedules, restarts, scales and service-discovers hundreds of containers across nodes.

nodes.label: Cloud-Native
nodes.rationale: A design philosophy built for instances that appear and disappear, not merely running old software on a cloud.

nodes.label: Provider Rate Limit Is the Real Ceiling
nodes.norm_label: provider rate limit is the real ceiling
nodes.rationale: Throughput is the lowest in the chain (function concurrency, provider rate limit, database); scaling functions without capping rate yields HTTP 429 storms.

nodes.label: Shared Kernel Weakens Isolation vs VM

nodes.label: 'Works on My Machine' Problem
nodes.rationale: Same image everywhere yields the same environment, like a sealed standard shipping container.

nodes.label: Orchestrator Adds Complexity; Not Always Worth It
nodes.norm_label: orchestrator adds complexity; not always worth it
nodes.rationale: Small teams with few containers may bear more operational burden than benefit.

nodes.label: ELK Stack (Elasticsearch)
nodes.rationale: Indexes every field of every log line for powerful full-text search at much higher storage/memory cost.

nodes.label: Grafana Loki
nodes.rationale: Deliberately indexes only a few labels (like Prometheus) and stores compressed log bodies, avoiding cardinality blow-up for far lower cost at the price of slower free-text search.

nodes.label: ELK Full-field Index Cost Trade-off
nodes.rationale: Teams choosing ELK for full-text power are often surprised by how fast storage cost grows with traffic and end up migrating to Loki or cutting retention.

nodes.label: Runbook
nodes.rationale: Short per-alert document with first checks and escalation, linking to relevant dashboards, reducing thinking time when woken at night.

nodes.label: Post-Incident Review
nodes.rationale: Abnormally high burn rate warrants a review; results feed back into new metrics, dashboards, and runbooks, closing the observability loop.

nodes.label: One Dashboard One Audience
nodes.rationale: A dashboard serving executives and on-call at once ends up used by nobody because each group scrolls past irrelevant panels; split into overview and drill-down.

nodes.label: Match Visualization Type to Question
nodes.rationale: Time-series for trends, single stat/gauge for current value vs threshold, heatmap for distributions, table/bar for comparisons. Trap: single stat of average latency hides p95/p99 detail; use multi-percentile time-series.

nodes.label: Conventional Commits
nodes.rationale: Machine-readable commit prefixes (feat/fix/BREAKING CHANGE) let tools decide the SemVer bump and changelog without human judgment, removing manual error.

nodes.label: Release Automation
nodes.rationale: Manual changelog writing and version decisions are tedious and error-prone; automating from commit history is consistent.

nodes.label: Commit Convention Enforcement at Scale
nodes.rationale: Conventions without enforcement decay; need immediate feedback loop at commit time plus CI backstop.

nodes.label: Clean Architecture
nodes.rationale: Concentric circles (Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks and Drivers) instead of straight layers, so business logic is independent of framework, DB and UI.

nodes.label: Clean Architecture as Over-Engineering
nodes.rationale: Full Clean Architecture costs interfaces, DI and a composition root; not worth it for small CRUD apps. Pays off with complex business logic and frequent infrastructure swaps.

nodes.label: Strategy Justified Despite YAGNI
nodes.rationale: YAGNI applies only without a real signal for variation; rate limiting is a domain with known multiple algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket) with different trade-offs, so a swappable interface up front is justified.

nodes.label: Balancing Loop (B)
nodes.rationale: Goal-seeking feedback that resists change and pulls the system back toward a target; the mechanism of stability.

nodes.label: Reinforcing Loop (R)
nodes.rationale: Has no goal of its own and amplifies in the same direction until something else (resources, saturation, a balancing loop) stops it; not inherently bad.

nodes.label: Goal-Seeking Behavior
nodes.rationale: Signature of predictable, controllable systems: a strong B loop without excessive delay self-corrects toward an acceptable state.

nodes.label: Structure Produces Behavior
nodes.rationale: A tiny difference in the update equation (reinforce vs. close the gap) yields completely different long-run behavior.

nodes.label: Linear Intuition Trap
nodes.rationale: Human intuition predicts linearly, so early exponential growth looks slow and teams delay response until too late.

nodes.label: Loop Strength Trade-off in Goal-Seeking
nodes.rationale: Too weak a loop converges painfully slowly; too strong a loop overshoots and oscillates.

nodes.label: S-Curve Forecasting Trap
nodes.rationale: The first half of an S-curve looks exactly like exponential growth, so teams over-forecast capacity and targets.

nodes.label: Abstraction
nodes.rationale: Design decision about what to expose versus hide; encapsulation is the mechanism (wall) that makes the abstraction (blueprint) real.

nodes.label: Encapsulation
nodes.rationale: Bundle data with behavior and restrict direct access so rules (validation) are enforced at the single point where data changes.

nodes.label: Cohesion
nodes.rationale: Measures how related methods and data inside one module are.

nodes.label: Low Coupling + High Cohesion Goal
nodes.rationale: Both are needed together: high cohesion with high coupling still ripples changes; low coupling with low cohesion scatters logic.

nodes.label: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
nodes.rationale: One reason to change means one actor/stakeholder owns the logic; ties to high cohesion.

nodes.label: Builder Pattern
nodes.rationale: Separate step-by-step construction from the finished object and validate once at build().

nodes.label: Builder Overuse Warning
nodes.rationale: Builder adds boilerplate; only worth it for many (4-5+) fields with optional values or complex validation.

nodes.label: eBPF Business Context Blind Spot
nodes.rationale: eBPF cannot know user, order or checkout context; that requires span attributes written in code via OpenTelemetry, so the two approaches complement rather than replace each other.

nodes.label: eBPF
nodes.rationale: Sandboxed, verified programs in the Linux kernel hook syscalls and packets, observing every process without modifying application code; covers legacy services but sees only network/syscall level.

nodes.label: Continuous Profiling
nodes.rationale: Always-on low-overhead sampling profiling in production, retaining flame graphs for before/after comparison to find regressions that only appear in production.

nodes.label: Metric to Trace to Profile Investigation Ladder
nodes.norm_label: metric to trace to profile investigation ladder
nodes.rationale: Metric says there is a problem, trace says which service, profile says which function; stopping at metric+trace leaves no code-level target.

nodes.label: Flame Graph Diff Before/After Deploy
nodes.rationale: Comparing flame graphs before and after a deploy pinpoints the function whose time grew, without adding log lines or reproducing the issue.

nodes.label: Sampling Profiler
nodes.rationale: Trades 100% fidelity for very low overhead by sampling call stacks periodically (e.g. every 10ms); slow functions are sampled more often so results are statistically accurate.

nodes.label: Castle-and-Moat Security Model
nodes.rationale: Perimeter (firewall/VPN) trust model: anyone inside the network is trusted; low overhead but a single credential leak exposes everything.

nodes.label: STRIDE

nodes.label: Trust Boundary
nodes.rationale: Dashed line drawn over the architecture diagram where data crosses from an untrusted to a trusted zone; STRIDE is asked at each crossing.

nodes.label: Dependency Signing / Provenance
nodes.rationale: Trust verifiable signatures rather than matching name/version; provenance records which source and build system produced the artifact. Protects against unknown threats that scanners cannot detect.

nodes.label: SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)
nodes.rationale: Manifest of every dependency and exact version per build (Syft, CycloneDX); turns 'are we affected?' from manual audit into a database query.

nodes.label: ADR: mTLS between internal services instead of trusting network boundary
nodes.norm_label: adr: mtls between internal services instead of trusting network boundary
nodes.rationale: A malware-infected laptop on the VPN called internal APIs freely; decision: every service-to-service call uses mTLS. Trade-off: certificate rotation burden and TLS handshake latency.

nodes.label: Zero Trust Architecture
nodes.rationale: Never trust, always verify: unit of trust shifts from network location to identity + context of each request, because one breached point otherwise allows free lateral movement.

nodes.label: ADR: Field-level encryption for credit card data
nodes.norm_label: adr: field-level encryption for credit card data
nodes.rationale: Auditor noted a directly breached database would leak plaintext cards despite firewall/WAF/auth; encrypt at field level with separate key management. Trade-off: query complexity and encrypt/decrypt overhead.

nodes.label: Defense Diversity
nodes.rationale: Layers must use different mechanisms closing different vulnerability classes; two firewalls bypassed the same way are not independent layers.

nodes.label: Defense in Depth
nodes.rationale: Layer multiple independent protections (like submarine watertight compartments) so one breached layer does not collapse everything. Example: WAF plus parameterized queries, since the WAF can be bypassed by unknown payloads.

nodes.label: ADR: Threat modeling before building Payment Service
nodes.norm_label: adr: threat modeling before building payment service
nodes.rationale: Prior system had an elevation-of-privilege flaw on the refund API; STRIDE review before coding found 3 design issues at the cost of about 2 extra design days per big feature.

nodes.label: Threat Modeling

nodes.label: ADR: Move DB credentials from env vars to Secrets Manager

nodes.label: Least Privilege
nodes.rationale: Every service, user and API key gets only the permissions needed, limiting blast radius if compromised.

nodes.label: Secrets Management
nodes.rationale: Applications fetch short-lived credentials from a Secrets Manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) at runtime instead of hardcoding them.

nodes.label: Secure by Design
nodes.rationale: Security is part of the architecture from the blueprint, not a feature bolted on later.

nodes.label: Trust Boundary Design
nodes.rationale: Threat modeling finds where trust boundaries are; secure by design makes every crossing validated, authenticated and sanitized from the start.

nodes.label: ADR: SBOM generation and dependency signature verification in CI
nodes.norm_label: adr: sbom generation and dependency signature verification in ci
nodes.rationale: A critical CVE took 2 days of manual audit to scope; CI now emits an SBOM per build and verifies signatures, cutting audit to minutes at the cost of slightly longer builds and some unsigned dependencies needing replacement.

nodes.label: Supply Chain Security
nodes.rationale: Risk extends beyond own code to dependencies, base images and build pipeline tools; one compromised library infects every dependent app even with bug-free own code.

nodes.label: Remote Write

nodes.label: Append-only Time-Series Storage

nodes.rationale: Accepted: readable code mapping to business talk, at the cost of refactoring all call sites and renaming when vocabulary changes.

nodes.label: Bounded Context
nodes.rationale: Ubiquitous Language is only consistent inside one Bounded Context; 'order' in Sales (price, discount) differs from 'order' in Shipping (address, tracking).

nodes.label: Ubiquitous Language
nodes.rationale: One vocabulary shared by domain experts, docs and code removes the translation layer; bugs live in the gap where e.g. status 4 means different things to different people, so code is refactored whenever business vocabulary shifts.

nodes.label: ADR: Use ACL When Integrating Legacy Accounting
nodes.norm_label: adr: use acl when integrating legacy accounting
nodes.rationale: Accepted: keeps domain clean and aligned with Ubiquitous Language, at the cost of maintaining adapter code and updating it when legacy format changes.

nodes.label: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)
nodes.rationale: A translation layer so a bad or mismatched external model never leaks into our domain model; used for legacy and low-trust third parties.

nodes.label: Context Mapping
nodes.rationale: The set of relationship patterns between bounded contexts: who has bargaining power, who adapts to whom, and how to defend against untrusted models.

nodes.label: Generic setStatus(order, 4) Anti-pattern
nodes.rationale: Magic status codes force a translation layer and cause misinterpretation bugs; new hires need a human translator.

nodes.label: Choose Pattern by Bargaining Power and Model Trust
nodes.norm_label: choose pattern by bargaining power and model trust
nodes.rationale: Two axes decide: can we negotiate API changes, and is the other side's model clean enough to use directly; if not negotiable or untrusted, build an ACL.

nodes.label: ADR: Redesign Payment Security After Pentest
nodes.norm_label: adr: redesign payment security after pentest

nodes.label: Defense in Depth
nodes.rationale: Independent, diverse layers (network, identity, application, data, monitoring); a second WAF doing the same job is not depth.

nodes.label: Quality Attributes Compete (Cannot Max All)
nodes.rationale: ilities compete for resources and complexity: security costs performance, availability costs maintainability, microservice scalability costs testability; architect must choose and consciously trade.

nodes.label: Consistency Chosen Per Use Case
nodes.rationale: Payment must be strongly consistent; stock display can be eventual but the actual reservation must be strong.

nodes.label: 'Inside the VPN Means Trusted' Assumption
nodes.rationale: Being on the same network is not identity; one compromised service gives the attacker every internal API.

nodes.label: Zero Trust and Layers Cost Latency and Ops
nodes.norm_label: zero trust and layers cost latency and ops
nodes.rationale: mTLS handshake adds latency per call and independent layers add certificate and secrets rotation, audit log operations.

nodes.label: ADR: Strangler Fig Starting at Stock Lookup
nodes.norm_label: adr: strangler fig starting at stock lookup
nodes.rationale: Accepted: features ship incrementally with no downtime; cost is operating a facade and monitoring old and new in parallel.

nodes.label: Architecture Erosion
nodes.rationale: Accumulated shortcuts over years, plus absence of automated boundary checks and tests, produce a big ball of mud nobody dares touch.

nodes.label: Facade as Single Point of Failure
nodes.norm_label: facade as single point of failure

nodes.label: Shadow Comparison of Old vs New
nodes.norm_label: shadow comparison of old vs new

nodes.label: Strangler Fig Pattern
nodes.rationale: Put a facade in front of the monolith and migrate one capability at a time so every step is small enough to roll back instantly.

nodes.label: ADR-001: Isolate Undocumented Queue Consumer as Container
nodes.norm_label: adr-001: isolate undocumented queue consumer as container

nodes.label: Pick Lowest-risk, Clearest-boundary Capability First
nodes.rationale: Read-only Stock Lookup proves the approach cheaply; starting with high-value but tightly coupled write capabilities risks losing trust in the strangler approach.

nodes.label: Start ADR Habit With First Change
nodes.norm_label: start adr habit with first change

nodes.label: Running System as Source of Truth
nodes.norm_label: running system as source of truth
nodes.rationale: The live system cannot lie, unlike memory; use people only to confirm intent ('why'), not structure ('what').

nodes.label: Cross-Cutting Concern
nodes.rationale: retry/timeout/encryption/metrics ถูกเขียนซ้ำในทุก service แบบไม่สม่ำเสมอ และแก้ policy กลางต้องไล่แก้ทีละ service ทีละภาษา

nodes.label: mTLS (Mutual TLS)
nodes.rationale: พิสูจน์ตัวตนทั้งสองฝั่ง ไม่เชื่อใครแม้อยู่ใน network เดียวกัน; sidecar ออกและหมุนเวียน certificate อัตโนมัติ

nodes.label: Traffic Shaping (Canary / Weighted Routing)
nodes.rationale: ของแถมเมื่อ traffic ผ่าน sidecar อยู่แล้ว — สั่งสัดส่วน traffic จาก control plane โดยไม่แตะโค้ด application

nodes.label: Long-Lived Feature Branch
nodes.rationale: ต้นทุน merge เพิ่มแบบไม่เป็นเชิงเส้น และทดสอบ integration ไม่ได้ระหว่างทาง

nodes.label: Service Mesh
nodes.rationale: ย้าย cross-cutting concern (retry, mTLS, metrics) ออกจากโค้ด application ไปชั้น infrastructure ให้ control plane บังคับ policy เดียวกันทุก sidecar; แลกด้วย latency เพิ่มและภาระดูแล control plane — คุ้มเมื่อจำนวน service มากพอที่ความไม่สม่ำเสมอเป็นปัญหาใหญ่กว่า

nodes.label: Sidecar Proxy (Envoy)
nodes.rationale: รัน proxy เป็น container ข้าง service ใน Pod เดียวกัน ดักทุก connection โดยโค้ด application ไม่ต้องรู้ ไม่ว่าเขียนด้วยภาษาอะไร

nodes.label: Strangler Fig Pattern
nodes.rationale: migrate legacy ทีละ capability ผ่าน facade โดยระบบใช้งานได้ตลอด rollback ได้ทีละชิ้น หลีกเลี่ยงความเสี่ยงทั้งระบบของ big-bang rewrite

nodes.label: Branch by Abstraction
nodes.rationale: วาง interface หน้า implementation เดิมแล้วสร้างของใหม่หลัง interface บน main ตลอด ไม่มี branch ยาวให้ drift; ทำงานระดับ component

nodes.label: Parallel Run (Dark Launch / Shadow Traffic)
nodes.rationale: รัน old/new คู่ขนานบน traffic จริง ตอบ user จาก old แล้ว diff ผล new เพื่อหา edge case ที่ test นึกไม่ถึงโดยไม่กระทบผู้ใช้

nodes.label: Architecture Erosion
nodes.rationale: ช่องว่างระหว่างสถาปัตยกรรมที่ตั้งใจกับที่มีจริง เกิดจากทางลัดเล็กๆ สะสมโดยไม่มีใครตัดสินใจทำลาย boundary

nodes.label: Technical Debt as a Stock
nodes.rationale: inflow = ทางลัดตอน deadline, outflow = เวลา refactor; ถ้าไม่มี outflow stock สะสมไม่มีวันลด

nodes.label: Fitness Function
nodes.rationale: unit test สำหรับสถาปัตยกรรม — แปลงการตัดสินใจเชิงสถาปัตยกรรมเป็นกฎที่เครื่องตรวจอัตโนมัติใน CI/CD เพื่อไม่พึ่งวินัยหรือความจำของคน; ใช้ได้เฉพาะสิ่งที่วัดได้และ threshold ไม่ควรเข้มเกินจนทีม bypass

nodes.label: Intentional Technical Debt
nodes.rationale: debt ที่ทีมตัดสินใจร่วมกัน บันทึกเป็น ADR มีแผนจ่ายคืน ต่างจาก erosion ที่ไม่มีใครรู้ตัว

nodes.label: Refactoring Time Allocation (e.g. 20% time)
nodes.rationale: เปิด outflow valve เพื่อไม่ให้ tech debt สะสม overshoot

nodes.label: Delay
nodes.rationale: People overlook that a delay exists between changing a flow and seeing its effect on the observed stock, so they decide again too early.

nodes.label: Delay Notation on Causal Loop Diagram
nodes.norm_label: delay notation on causal loop diagram

nodes.label: Oscillation
nodes.rationale: Balancing loop plus delay: the system corrects from stale information and so must correct back again, repeatedly.

nodes.label: Overcorrection from Unrecognized Delay
nodes.rationale: Seeing no immediate effect, people decide again harder; when both effects arrive together the result overshoots the need.

nodes.label: Over-strong or Delayed B Loop Oscillates
nodes.norm_label: over-strong or delayed b loop oscillates
nodes.rationale: A balancing loop does not guarantee stillness; strength and delay decide between smooth settling and repeated overshoot.

nodes.label: Which Loop Is Stronger and When
nodes.norm_label: which loop is stronger and when
nodes.rationale: Both R and B loops always coexist; what matters is which is stronger at a given time, which delay can swing.

nodes.label: Flat Key Namespace / HTTP API Access
nodes.norm_label: flat key namespace / http api access

nodes.label: Presigned URL
nodes.rationale: Client uploads directly to storage with a short-lived, path-scoped signature so the app server is not a throughput bottleneck.

nodes.label: Files in Object Storage, URL in Database
nodes.norm_label: files in object storage, url in database
nodes.rationale: Big blobs in a DB slow backup, burden replication and cost far more per GB.

nodes.label: Password Hashing (bcrypt, argon2)
nodes.rationale: One-way; unlike encryption it cannot be reversed even with a key.

nodes.label: Limited-Scope Revocable Delegated Access
nodes.rationale: User password never reaches the app; app gets scoped, revocable key.

nodes.label: Read:Write Ratio
nodes.rationale: Read-heavy points to cache/read replica; write-heavy points to sharding/message queue.

nodes.label: Base62 Encoding of Auto-Increment ID
nodes.rationale: Guaranteed unique in one step; random-then-check needs a DB round trip and collides more as namespace fills.

nodes.label: Key-Value / NoSQL Store Choice
nodes.rationale: Data is only short_code to long_url with no joins; SQL features are unused overhead.

nodes.label: Stateless App Servers behind Load Balancer
nodes.norm_label: stateless app servers behind load balancer

nodes.label: Redis Cache (short_code to URL)
nodes.rationale: Sub-millisecond vs 5-20ms DB read; DB touched only on cache miss.

nodes.label: Back-of-Envelope / Order of Magnitude
nodes.rationale: One order of magnitude difference changes the right architecture; exactness is unnecessary.

nodes.label: Shard Only When Needed
nodes.rationale: Single indexed machine handles tens to hundreds of millions of rows; earlier sharding is over-engineering.

nodes.label: Goals (Level 3)
nodes.rationale: Changing the system goal realigns every decision automatically.

nodes.label: Information Flows (Level 6)
nodes.rationale: Who sees what data and when; real-time deploy dashboard speeds team response.

nodes.label: Paradigm (Level 2)
nodes.rationale: The mindset the system rests on (deploy is a risk vs deploy is routine); changing it changes team culture, not just one rule.

nodes.label: Rules (Level 5)
nodes.rationale: Rules, incentives, constraints change whole-team behavior immediately without relying on individual discipline (e.g. CI must be green before merge).

nodes.label: Three Leverage Groups: Parameters / Structure / Goals & Paradigm
nodes.norm_label: three leverage groups: parameters / structure / goals & paradigm
nodes.rationale: The 12 levels collapse into Parameters (12-9), Structure (8-4), Goals & Paradigm (3-1) for fast decisions.

nodes.label: On-call Dashboard + Recurring-Incident Rule (partial structure fix)
nodes.norm_label: on-call dashboard + recurring-incident rule (partial structure fix)
nodes.rationale: Showing on-call load to executives and forcing sprint capacity for incidents recurring over 3 times/month reduced incidents but on-call stayed heavier than other teams.

nodes.label: Paradigm Example: Employee as Cost vs Asset
nodes.norm_label: paradigm example: employee as cost vs asset
nodes.rationale: Same rules, different paradigm steers every sub-decision in opposite directions.

nodes.label: Senior Engineer Switching Paradigms
nodes.rationale: Juniors apply one learned frame to all problems; seniors treat normalize/denormalize and monolith/microservices as tools with context-dependent cost-benefit.

nodes.label: Transcending Paradigms (Level 1)
nodes.rationale: Realizing no paradigm is absolute truth and switching lenses by context; highest leverage because it changes how questions are asked, hardest because people tie paradigms to identity.

nodes.label: Iceberg Level 4: Mental Models
nodes.rationale: Deep beliefs that caused the structure to be built that way; hardest to change but widest, most lasting effect.

nodes.label: Definition of Done Includes Complexity Limit
nodes.norm_label: definition of done includes complexity limit
nodes.rationale: Goal/mental-model fix acting on inflow: work adding excess complexity is not done - closing the tap rather than widening the drain.

nodes.label: Belief: Refactor Is Not Real Work
nodes.norm_label: belief: refactor is not real work
nodes.rationale: Refactor is seen as spare-time work so it loses every prioritization contest and the outflow never opens.

nodes.label: Correlation ID (req_id)
nodes.rationale: Same ID stamped on every log line of a request across services; flat grouping with no timing or parent-child structure.

nodes.label: Structured Logging
nodes.rationale: Logs with discrete fields can be queried, filtered and aggregated reliably; unlike free-text logs they do not silently break when message wording changes.

nodes.label: Exemplar
nodes.rationale: A trace_id attached to a metric sample so you can jump from a latency spike straight to the real trace instead of guessing by time window.

nodes.label: Distributed Tracing
nodes.rationale: Extends correlation IDs with start/end timing and parent-child relationships so you can see which service consumes the most time.

nodes.label: Trace Context Propagation
nodes.rationale: Each service must read incoming context and forward it, or downstream services start disconnected traces.

nodes.label: Bounded-cardinality Label Rule
nodes.rationale: Only use labels with a limited, roughly known set of values (method, status, service); move unbounded per-user/request detail to logs or traces.

nodes.label: Unstructured Log Regex Fragility
nodes.rationale: Editing a log message wording silently breaks regex-based alerts and dashboards.

nodes.label: Metric-Trace-Log Correlation Workflow
nodes.rationale: Works only if all systems share one trace_id end-to-end and trace context is propagated; otherwise correlation reverts to time-window guessing.

nodes.label: Log vs Trace Complementarity
nodes.rationale: Metric says there is a problem, trace says where, log gives the exact detail.

nodes.label: Propagation Break at Message Queues
nodes.rationale: Async queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ) drop context unless traceparent is attached to message headers; consumers otherwise start a new trace.

nodes.label: CQRS Intensity Levels (separate query objects / views / separate DB)
nodes.norm_label: cqrs intensity levels (separate query objects / views / separate db)

nodes.label: Current-State Storage (UPDATE in place)
nodes.rationale: เก็บเฉพาะค่าล่าสุด ประวัติหายเมื่อถูกเขียนทับ — รู้ว่า "ตอนนี้เป็นอะไร" แต่ไม่รู้ "ทำไม"

nodes.label: Multiple Read Models from One Event Stream
nodes.norm_label: multiple read models from one event stream

nodes.label: Costs of CQRS / Event Sourcing
nodes.rationale: eventual consistency, ส่วนประกอบเพิ่ม (write store, read store, projector, snapshot), debug ยากขึ้น, learning curve สูง

nodes.label: Event Versioning
nodes.rationale: event เก่าแก้ไม่ได้เพราะ append-only แต่ consumer ต้องรับมือ shape ต่างกันไปตลอดกาล

nodes.label: Snapshot Logic Drifting from Replay Logic
nodes.norm_label: snapshot logic drifting from replay logic
nodes.rationale: ให้ snapshot logic เรียก apply function ตัวเดียวกับ replay เพื่อกันบั๊กซ่อนใน code path ที่ถูกใช้น้อย

nodes.label: Snapshot Store (snapshotting at scale)
nodes.rationale: เก็บแยกจาก event log key ด้วย aggregate id + version; ความถี่เป็น trade-off ระหว่างพื้นที่กับเวลา replay

nodes.label: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
nodes.rationale: แยกโมเดลเขียน (ถูกต้อง, normalized) ออกจากโมเดลอ่าน (เร็ว, denormalized) เพราะ read/write ratio เหลื่อมกันมากและ scale แยกกันได้; ต้นทุนคือ eventual consistency และความซับซ้อน — ไม่ควรใช้ถ้าระบบเล็กและ query ยังเร็วพอ

nodes.label: Event Sourcing
nodes.rationale: เก็บลำดับเหตุการณ์แบบ append-only เป็น source of truth แล้ว derive current state ด้วย replay — ได้ audit trail และ time travel ฟรี; ต่างจาก audit log ตรงที่ไม่มี current state แยกต่างหากเป็นความจริง

nodes.label: Snapshot
nodes.rationale: จดสรุป state เป็นระยะ แล้ว replay เฉพาะ event หลัง snapshot ล่าสุด เพื่อไม่ให้ replay จากต้นทุกครั้ง

nodes.label: Event Log as Source of Truth
nodes.norm_label: event log as source of truth

nodes.label: CQRS + Event Sourcing Combination
nodes.rationale: แต่ละอย่างแก้ปัญหาที่อีกฝั่งทิ้งไว้: ES เก็บความจริงระยะยาว, CQRS ให้แต่ละหน้าจออ่านเร็วตรงความต้องการ; จับคู่แล้วสร้าง read model ใหม่ย้อนหลังได้ด้วย replay

nodes.label: Rebuild Read Model by Replaying Events
nodes.norm_label: rebuild read model by replaying events
nodes.rationale: เขียน projector ใหม่แล้ว replay event ทั้งหมดก็ได้ read model รูปแบบใหม่ครบถ้วน โดยไม่ต้องรื้อฝั่ง write

nodes.label: Using a Powerful Pattern in the Wrong Place
nodes.norm_label: using a powerful pattern in the wrong place
nodes.rationale: ใช้ event sourcing กับ CRUD รายชื่อพนักงานเพิ่มภาระโดยไม่มีประโยชน์ — เพิ่มความซับซ้อนได้เมื่อแก้ปัญหาจริงเท่านั้น

nodes.label: When to Use CQRS/ES (decision criteria)
nodes.rationale: คุ้มเมื่อมี audit/compliance เข้มงวด, ต้องการ read model หลายรูปแบบมาก หรือ read/write ratio สุดขั้ว — ไม่ใช่เพราะ pattern ฟังดูทันสมัย

nodes.label: Upcasting
nodes.rationale: แปลง event เก่าเป็น shape ล่าสุดตอนอ่านที่ deserialization layer จุดเดียว ไม่แตะข้อมูลที่เก็บ; consumer เห็นแต่เวอร์ชันล่าสุด; ต้องดูแล upcaster ของทุก shape ตลอดไป

nodes.label: Weak Schema Evolution
nodes.rationale: จำกัดการแก้ event ให้เพิ่ม optional field เท่านั้น ไม่ต้องเขียน transform แต่ต้องใช้วินัยทีมสูง ผิดกฎครั้งเดียว event เก่าพังทั้งหมด

nodes.label: Invite Feature Growth Dominance Shift Case
nodes.norm_label: invite feature growth dominance shift case

nodes.label: Loop Dominance
nodes.rationale: Which loop currently controls system behavior; a dominance shift happens when a weak loop that existed all along gains enough strength.

nodes.label: Carrying Capacity
nodes.rationale: No real exponential growth continues forever; a natural limit always waits ahead.

nodes.label: Overshoot and Collapse
nodes.rationale: An R loop outruns the B loop that should brake it (delayed perception or missing loop), blows past carrying capacity, then crashes.

nodes.label: Inflection Point
nodes.rationale: R and B loops are equally strong here and growth rate peaks; capacity planning should target this point.

nodes.label: S-Shaped Growth (Logistic Growth)
nodes.rationale: Exponential growth meeting goal-seeking: R loop dominates early, B loop strengthens until the curve flattens smoothly at carrying capacity.

nodes.label: Limits to Growth
nodes.rationale: Dangerous because the balancing loop is negligible at first and only becomes noticeable near the limit, usually too late to slow down.

nodes.label: Why Dominance Shift Is Hard to Predict
nodes.norm_label: why dominance shift is hard to predict
nodes.rationale: The loop about to dominate is too small to notice while the current loop is strong; attention follows present impact, not future potential.

nodes.label: Collapse Steeper Than Growth
nodes.rationale: After the limit is hit a second reinforcing loop (users fleeing, confidence draining) runs in reverse on top of the first.

nodes.label: Find Limits Before the System Does
nodes.norm_label: find limits before the system does
nodes.rationale: Capacity planning, load testing and early-warning alerts build a timely balancing loop instead of discovering limits by failure.

nodes.label: Expand the Constraint Before Pushing Growth
nodes.norm_label: expand the constraint before pushing growth
nodes.rationale: Pushing the R loop harder only hits the limit faster; find and widen the constraining condition first.

nodes.label: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
nodes.rationale: Subtype must be behaviorally substitutable for base type, not just type-signature compatible; mathematical is-a is not behavioral is-a.

nodes.label: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
nodes.rationale: Clients should not depend on methods they do not use; split fat interfaces by real capability.

nodes.label: Transparent vs Safe Composite
nodes.rationale: Transparent puts add() in the shared interface (leaf throws), safe separates a Container interface; trade-off between client convenience and type safety, clashing with ISP.

nodes.label: Workload Shape Drives Architecture (Twitter vs Instagram)
nodes.norm_label: workload shape drives architecture (twitter vs instagram)
nodes.rationale: Twitter fan-out concentrates load on celebrity accounts, so a monolith broke early; Instagram's evenly spread workload stayed monolithic. Do not add complexity before the real problem arrives, but do not fear it when needed; split only measured bottlenecks, incrementally, not by trend.

nodes.label: ADR: Start E-commerce with a Monolith First
nodes.norm_label: adr: start e-commerce with a monolith first
nodes.rationale: 4 engineers, unknown domain boundaries, MVP speed: one modular monolith, revisit splitting by Conway's Law if team grows past ~15.

nodes.label: Event-Driven Architecture
nodes.rationale: Producers publish events and finish; subscribers handle them independently, so notification slowness or outage cannot cascade into Order/Payment.

nodes.label: Sync on Money Path, Events for the Rest
nodes.norm_label: sync on money path, events for the rest
nodes.rationale: Customer must know the outcome now on reserve-and-charge, so Order orchestrates synchronously; confirmation email, warehouse notice and loyalty points are announced as events.

nodes.label: Four Golden Signals
nodes.rationale: Google SRE's minimal metric set (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) every service should have on its main dashboard before service-specific metrics.

nodes.label: p95/p99 Percentile Latency
nodes.rationale: Averages hide outliers; percentiles reflect the experience of the worst-served users.

nodes.label: Utilization vs Saturation
nodes.rationale: Utilization is percent in use; saturation is whether the resource can take more work (growing queue length signals saturation even at 70% CPU).

nodes.label: RED Method (Rate, Errors, Duration)
nodes.rationale: Service-centric, request-driven view; the user-facing symptom view, suited to SLOs.

nodes.label: USE Method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors)
nodes.rationale: Resource-centric view (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network) used to find which resource is the bottleneck.

nodes.label: Latency Averaging Trap (success vs error)
nodes.rationale: Failed requests often fail fast, so blending them with successful latency makes numbers look better than reality; measure success latency separately and track error rate on its own.

nodes.label: RED then USE Investigation Flow
nodes.rationale: RED shows the symptom users feel; USE finds the sick organ (e.g. checkout error rate spike traced to DB disk I/O saturation).

nodes.label: Log Shipper (Filebeat, Fluentd, Promtail)
nodes.rationale: Runs beside each service and forwards logs so service does not write directly to storage and network failures do not hurt the main service.

nodes.label: Span
nodes.rationale: One unit of work in a trace with start time, end time, span ID and parent span; a child starts after and ends before its parent.

nodes.label: OTel Collector
nodes.rationale: Separates processing/export from the app so backend, sampling and PII scrubbing can change from one place without redeploying apps.

nodes.label: Manual Instrumentation
nodes.rationale: Needed for business-logic spans (e.g. validate order) that auto-instrumentation cannot see.

nodes.label: Parallel Spans Timing Trap
nodes.rationale: Parallel child spans mean parent duration is not the sum of children; read the waterfall for overlaps.

nodes.label: Vendor Lock-in in Tracing Libraries
nodes.rationale: Vendor-specific tracing libraries forced re-instrumenting all code to switch backends; OTel's vendor-neutral API removes that.

nodes.label: Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting
nodes.rationale: Combine short and long windows to confirm a real, sustained problem: short window catches fast, long window filters transient spikes.

nodes.label: Alert Fatigue
nodes.rationale: Non-actionable, frequently firing alerts cause people to ignore notifications, so genuinely important alerts get ignored too (car alarm in the wind analogy).

nodes.label: On-Call Rotation
nodes.rationale: Rotate primary on-call (e.g. weekly) so no single person burns out.

nodes.label: Dashboard Overload
nodes.rationale: Adding a panel for every new question yields 50+ panels nobody scans; people start ignoring important panels. Prune unused panels periodically.

nodes.label: Every Alert Must Be Actionable
nodes.rationale: An alert that wakes someone at night must have something they can do immediately; otherwise downgrade to a dashboard or ticket.

nodes.label: Everything-Is-a-Page Anti-pattern
nodes.rationale: New teams set all alerts to Page 'just in case', exhausting on-call so real incidents get slow response or muted alerts.

nodes.label: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

nodes.label: Error Budget
nodes.rationale: Acceptable failure quota = 100% - SLO target (99.9% SLO means 0.1% budget).

nodes.label: SLI (Service Level Indicator)
nodes.rationale: Measured value tied directly to user experience, e.g. % of requests answered successfully within 500ms; derived from Golden Signals metrics but over a rolling window.

nodes.label: SLI/SLO Dashboard Layout
nodes.rationale: Executives should see SLI vs SLO because raw error rate has no context for 'how bad is bad'; panels: current SLI vs target, 30-day trend with target line, error budget remaining.

nodes.label: SLO (Service Level Objective)
nodes.rationale: Target set for an SLI, e.g. SLI >= 99.9% over rolling 30 days.

nodes.label: Error Budget Burn Rate
nodes.rationale: Rate budget is consumed relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at end of SLO window; 1x = on plan, 100x = budget gone in hours. Alerts earlier than waiting for SLI to drop below SLO.

nodes.label: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
nodes.rationale: Customer-facing contract with business/legal consequences (e.g. refund below threshold).

nodes.label: Four Golden Signals at Top of Dashboard
nodes.norm_label: four golden signals at top of dashboard
nodes.rationale: Golden signals answer the first question everyone asks ('is it normal now?') fastest, so they sit above business-specific and debug panels.

nodes.label: Unrealistic SLO Trap
nodes.rationale: SLO set higher than the system ever achieved (e.g. 99.99%) makes the budget permanently exhausted and the dashboard permanently red, so the team ignores it; base SLOs on historical data and business tolerance.

nodes.label: Burn Rate Alert vs Static Error-Rate Threshold
nodes.norm_label: burn rate alert vs static error-rate threshold
nodes.rationale: Burn rate has a time dimension (time-to-exhaust), so severity can match urgency; a static threshold lacks it and gives false positives on short spikes.

nodes.label: Golden Signals to Burn Rate Chain
nodes.norm_label: golden signals to burn rate chain
nodes.rationale: Golden Signals measure -> SLI picks user-critical ones -> SLO sets target -> Error Budget computes quota -> Burn Rate alerts on abnormal consumption.

nodes.label: SLO Stricter Than SLA
nodes.rationale: Internal SLO is set tighter than the SLA so the team can react before the contractual SLA is breached (e.g. SLO 99.9% vs SLA 99.5%).

nodes.label: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
nodes.rationale: High-level business logic and low-level details both depend on abstractions; use where dependency direction matters, not on every class.

nodes.label: DIP Over-Abstraction Warning
nodes.rationale: Creating an interface for every class without planned swaps adds indirection without benefit.

nodes.label: Singleton Pattern
nodes.rationale: Guarantees one instance via private constructor plus static getInstance; valid when single instance is a true business requirement.

nodes.label: Singleton as Anti-Pattern
nodes.rationale: Problem is global static access that hides dependencies and blocks mocking, conflicting with DIP; keep one instance but inject it.

nodes.label: Progressive Delivery
nodes.rationale: Canary where the system, not a human, watches real metrics and decides to expand traffic or auto-rollback.

nodes.label: SLO-aligned Canary Metric Gate
nodes.rationale: Gate metrics must match SLO metrics (error rate, p99 latency via RED) rather than deploy success, so real user impact triggers rollback without human attention.

nodes.label: Chaos Engineering
nodes.rationale: Deliberate, controlled, hypothesis-driven failure experiments to verify that resilience mechanisms actually work before a real incident.

nodes.label: Incremental Blast Radius Expansion
nodes.rationale: Expand blast radius step by step only when the previous round passes; stop and fix at the first breach rather than jumping to worst-case.

nodes.label: Steady State Hypothesis
nodes.rationale: Define normal via RED/USE metrics and hypothesize they stay in bounds under fault; breaching bounds reveals a real weakness.

nodes.label: Weak Experiments Give False Confidence
nodes.rationale: Months of experiments with no findings may mean the faults are too mild (e.g. excess spare pods); escalate severity until the real resilience boundary is found.

nodes.label: Observability Cost Control (FinOps)
nodes.rationale: Collecting every log, metric and trace everywhere can cost more than the infrastructure observed; control cost per signal and across all three together.

nodes.label: Tiered Retention (hot/warm/cold)
nodes.rationale: New data is queried far more than old data, so move older data to slower, cheaper storage tiers instead of keeping everything on the most expensive tier.

nodes.label: Uniform Sampling Pitfall
nodes.rationale: A flat 1% sample across all levels may drop the logs of a rare (0.1%) incident entirely; sampling must respect data importance.

nodes.label: CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type)
nodes.rationale: Merges both sides automatically without discarding either; suits mergeable data such as a shopping cart.

nodes.label: Last-Write-Wins (LWW)
nodes.rationale: Simplest conflict resolution but silently drops the losing write.

nodes.label: Cross-Region Quorum
nodes.rationale: Majority confirmation across continents costs 100-200ms per write, so most systems accept LWW/CRDT conflicts instead.

nodes.label: Multi-Region Active-Active
nodes.rationale: All regions serve real traffic at once: survives region-level disaster and gives low latency via nearest region.

nodes.label: Cross-Region Write Conflict
nodes.rationale: Both regions accept a write locally before learning of the other, so replication must resolve conflicts.

nodes.label: Premature Service Split Risk
nodes.rationale: Splitting into services before the true business boundaries are known usually splits in the wrong place, and fixing it later is more expensive than keeping things together first.

nodes.label: ADR: API Gateway + Microservices Instead of New ESB

nodes.label: Wrong Boundaries Yield Chatty Pseudo-Monolith Services
nodes.norm_label: wrong boundaries yield chatty pseudo-monolith services

nodes.label: When to Prefer Modular Monolith over Microservices
