nodes.label: Consistency (ACID)
nodes.rationale: Data does not violate constraints within a single transaction; a different dimension from CAP consistency, so an ACID system can still be AP.

nodes.label: CAP Theorem
nodes.rationale: Partitions always happen in real distributed systems, so partition tolerance is mandatory; the real question is whether to choose Consistency or Availability when the network splits.

nodes.label: Consistency (CAP)
nodes.rationale: All nodes queried at the same time return exactly the same data (linearizability across machines).

nodes.label: Cassandra
nodes.rationale: Tunable per query between favoring latency or consistency.

nodes.label: DynamoDB
nodes.rationale: Chooses A on partition and L normally (speed first).

nodes.label: MongoDB
nodes.rationale: Default chooses C on partition and C normally (correctness first).

nodes.label: PACELC
nodes.rationale: Extends CAP: if Partition choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency. The Else case is far more common than partitions.

nodes.label: CP vs AP Choice
nodes.rationale: Banks lean CP (wrong balance is worse than slow service); social feeds lean AP. The choice can differ per operation or per dataset (e.g. CP for inventory, AP for product reviews), not one label for the whole system.

nodes.label: Distributed Monolith
nodes.rationale: Services split by shape but still tightly coupled (shared database, coordinated deploys), paying microservice costs without benefits; worse than the original monolith.

nodes.label: Microservices
nodes.rationale: Independent services with separate deploy and scaling, communicating over the network; split only when pain appears (slow deploys, coupled changes, uneven scaling, team boundaries).

nodes.label: Hidden Costs of Microservices
nodes.rationale: Network latency, partial failure, distributed transactions and operational overhead that were free inside a monolith.

nodes.label: Monolith
nodes.rationale: Single codebase and deployment with in-process calls; easy to start, debug and test but scales only as a whole. Most teams should start here.

nodes.label: Compensating Transaction
nodes.rationale: A real undo action (cancel hotel, cancel flight), not a database rollback.

nodes.label: Database Transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK)
nodes.rationale: Works within one database but cannot span the separate databases of multiple microservices.

nodes.label: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)
nodes.rationale: Locks resources across all databases until everyone votes, which is slow and deadlock-prone across networks; Saga is preferred for scaled microservices.

nodes.label: Modular Monolith
nodes.rationale: One deployable with clear internal module boundaries, making a later split into services much easier.

nodes.label: Saga Pattern
nodes.rationale: A chain of local transactions, each committed immediately, with compensating actions to undo earlier steps if a later one fails; trades atomicity for speed and no cross-service locks.

nodes.label: Semantic Lock
nodes.rationale: Business-level flag such as PENDING_CONFIRMATION marking a record as mid-saga so readers do not treat intermediate states (dirty reads) as final.

nodes.label: TTL (Time To Live)
nodes.rationale: short TTL: IP changes propagate fast but resolvers query constantly; long TTL: low load but a stale IP persists after a move until TTL expires

nodes.label: Cache invalidation is hard
nodes.rationale: knowing when to update the cached copy is harder than it looks; the industry jokes that it is one of two hard problems

nodes.label: Write-Back (Write-Behind)
nodes.rationale: write cache, acknowledge, sync DB later; fast but data is lost if the cache dies before syncing; fine for view counts or light analytics

nodes.label: Write-Through
nodes.rationale: write cache and DB together before acknowledging; always consistent but slower; suited to banking

nodes.label: Cache invalidation problem
nodes.rationale: real data changed but the cached copy (the price tag) still shows the old value

nodes.label: Index cost: faster reads, slower writes, more storage
nodes.norm_label: index cost: faster reads, slower writes, more storage
nodes.rationale: index only columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY; too many indexes bottleneck write-heavy tables

nodes.label: Selectivity
nodes.rationale: low-cardinality columns (e.g. boolean) barely narrow results so the index is not worth its cost and the DB may skip it; high-selectivity columns like email or UUID benefit most

nodes.label: What is worth caching
nodes.rationale: read-heavy data (read more than changed), expensive to compute, and tolerant of slightly stale values

nodes.label: TTL as a safety net
nodes.rationale: even with explicit invalidation, a short TTL guarantees a missed layer does not stay stale forever

nodes.label: Server-side in-memory cache
nodes.rationale: very fast but not shared with other server machines

nodes.label: Stale data across multiple cache layers
nodes.norm_label: stale data across multiple cache layers
nodes.rationale: each layer has its own TTL so different users may see different versions; fix with shorter TTL toward the user (CDN < Redis) or purge from inner to outer layer on important changes

nodes.label: Closer to the user = faster but harder to keep in sync
nodes.norm_label: closer to the user = faster but harder to keep in sync
nodes.rationale: large systems use all layers at once: CDN for static assets, Redis for shared frequently changing data, short-lived in-memory cache for heavy per-request computation

nodes.label: Causal Consistency
nodes.rationale: Guarantees causally related events are read in order (a reply is never seen before its parent comment), even though unrelated events may reorder.

nodes.label: Eventual Consistency
nodes.rationale: Any node answers immediately and data converges later; accepted for like counts, view counts, feeds where short staleness does not hurt correctness.

nodes.label: Inconsistency Window
nodes.rationale: Period when some replicas know the new value and others do not; good systems keep it to milliseconds or a few seconds.

nodes.label: Read-Your-Own-Writes
nodes.rationale: Middle ground: the writer immediately sees their own write even if others do not yet.

nodes.label: Vector Clock
nodes.rationale: Detects true happens-before ordering and concurrent conflicting writes, unlike wall-clock timestamps that drift between machines.

nodes.label: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA)
nodes.rationale: Services communicate by announcing events rather than direct commands, giving loose coupling, resilience and independent scaling at the cost of harder debugging, eventual consistency and event ordering/duplicate concerns. Real systems mix both styles.

nodes.label: Request-Driven (Direct Calls) Style
nodes.rationale: Caller must know every downstream service and slow or failed services stall the chain (tight coupling); still right when an immediate answer is needed, e.g. card authorization.

nodes.label: Cardinality Explosion
nodes.rationale: Tagging metrics with high-variety values like user_id creates millions of time series and can crash the monitoring system; use bounded tags and put per-user detail in logs or traces.

nodes.label: Structured Log
nodes.rationale: Detailed searchable event records with fields like req_id; too voluminous to store for every request at high traffic.

nodes.label: Metric
nodes.rationale: Cheap aggregated numbers over time (error rate, latency) tied to alert thresholds.

nodes.label: Observability
nodes.rationale: Answers how to know the system is failing and where; built on logs, metrics and traces used together.

nodes.label: Distributed Trace
nodes.rationale: A trace ID follows one request across services and renders as a waterfall of spans to find the slow hop.

nodes.label: Canary Deployment
nodes.rationale: Release to a small percentage first and watch metrics (error rate, latency) before expanding or rolling back; depends on good observability.

nodes.label: Metric then Trace then Log Investigation Flow
nodes.norm_label: metric then trace then log investigation flow
nodes.rationale: Metric shows there is a problem, trace shows where, log shows exactly what happened.

nodes.label: Feature Flag (Dark Launch)
nodes.rationale: Separates deploy from release: code ships dark behind a flag and is enabled per business rule without redeploying; downside is flag debt if old flags are not removed.

nodes.label: Client Polling Fallback
nodes.rationale: Client can query job status itself so results are not lost if a webhook delivery fails.

nodes.label: Dead Letter
nodes.rationale: Holding place for work that failed after all retries so the team can inspect it instead of losing it silently.

nodes.label: Webhook Signature Verification
nodes.rationale: Signed payload lets the receiver prove a webhook really came from the real server.

nodes.label: Synchronous Request
nodes.rationale: Client waits until the server finishes; heavy jobs (video encode) risk client timeout and tie up the server.

nodes.label: Webhook
nodes.rationale: Server calls the client's endpoint to deliver the result; can fail if the client is down, so it needs retries, dead letter and a polling fallback.

nodes.label: Dual Write Problem
nodes.rationale: Saving to the database and publishing to a queue are two separate writes; a crash between them leaves an order saved but nobody notified.

nodes.label: Message Queue
nodes.rationale: FIFO buffer between producer and consumer so both sides run at different speeds; consumers can be scaled horizontally and queued work survives a consumer failure. Examples: RabbitMQ, AWS SQS, Redis Streams.

nodes.label: Consumer Lag
nodes.rationale: Gap between latest published message and a consumer's position; if lag exceeds retention, unread messages are deleted, so lag must be monitored and consumers scaled.

nodes.label: Subscriber Offset
nodes.rationale: Each subscriber tracks its own read position so slow subscribers do not block fast ones.

nodes.label: Pub/Sub
nodes.rationale: One published message reaches all subscribers independently; the publisher need not know who listens, so adding a new subscriber needs no change to the publisher. Contrast with a queue where one consumer takes each message.

nodes.label: Retention Period
nodes.rationale: Pub/Sub topics keep messages for a limited time (Kafka default 7 days), unlike queues where messages stay until acked.

nodes.label: Batch Processing
nodes.rationale: Accumulate data then compute in one go: accurate and complete but slow; large systems usually run both stream and batch.

nodes.label: Out-of-Order Events
nodes.rationale: Network delay can make an earlier real-world event arrive after a later one, so closing windows immediately may drop late data.

nodes.label: Sliding Window
nodes.rationale: Overlapping windows that advance continuously; good for moving averages and smooth trends.

nodes.label: Stream Processing
nodes.rationale: Continuous computation on messages as they flow, giving seconds-level freshness; results may need correction when late data arrives.

nodes.label: Tumbling Window
nodes.rationale: Fixed non-overlapping time slices; each event belongs to exactly one window.

nodes.label: Watermark
nodes.rationale: Wait a bit before closing a window so late events can still arrive, trading freshness for accuracy.

nodes.label: Saga Choreography
nodes.rationale: Services publish events and react on their own with no central coordinator; the overall logic gets harder to trace as steps grow.

nodes.label: Accept-Then-Process-Later (Async Job) Pattern
nodes.rationale: Separate receiving the request from doing the work: respond immediately with a job_id, enqueue the work, let a worker process it, and notify later. Like a laundry shop receipt.

nodes.label: Transactional Outbox Pattern
nodes.rationale: Write an outbox row in the same DB transaction as the business data, and have a relay process publish it to the queue later, retrying safely because the record persists.

nodes.label: Speed-of-Light Network Latency Limit
nodes.rationale: Cross-continent round trips take at least roughly 100-200ms; within one data center under 1ms, so single-region systems rarely feel the L vs C trade-off.

nodes.label: Strong Consistency
nodes.rationale: Always reads the latest value with all nodes in agreement, at the cost of waiting for replica sync (higher latency); suited to bank balances and stock.

nodes.label: Availability Nines (99.9%, 99.99%)
nodes.rationale: No system has zero downtime; 99.9% is about 8.7 hours per year and 99.99% about 52 minutes.

nodes.label: Multi-Region Redundancy
nodes.rationale: Backup data center in another geography with cross-region replication; highest cost and complexity, used when downtime is extremely costly.

nodes.label: Latency vs Consistency Trade-off (Else case)
nodes.rationale: Even with a healthy network, answering fast from local data trades off against checking other nodes for a fresher answer; matters mainly in multi-region deployments.

nodes.label: Quorum Consistency (W + R > N)
nodes.rationale: If W write-acks plus R read-replicas exceed N copies, the write set and read set always overlap, guaranteeing the latest value is seen; W and R can be tuned for faster reads or writes.

nodes.label: Redundancy
nodes.rationale: No component should exist as a single copy: load balancers, database primaries, gateways and servers all need spares.

nodes.label: Backpressure
nodes.rationale: server sends faster than the client processes so buffers grow; fix by sampling/coalescing and sending only the latest value every short interval (e.g. 100ms)

nodes.label: Jitter and exponential backoff on reconnect
nodes.norm_label: jitter and exponential backoff on reconnect

nodes.label: Reconnect with sequence numbers
nodes.rationale: each event carries a sequence/message ID; after reconnecting the client reports the last ID it saw so the server resends only missed events

nodes.label: Reconnection storm
nodes.rationale: server restart drops many connections which all reconnect at once and spike the freshly restarted server

nodes.label: Cold cache on a newly added instance
nodes.norm_label: cold cache on a newly added instance
nodes.rationale: a new instance has an empty cache so full traffic makes every request miss and hammers the database; ramp traffic gradually like a canary rollout

nodes.label: Cache penetration
nodes.rationale: repeated lookups of keys that do not exist always miss the cache and hit the DB

nodes.label: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
nodes.rationale: a hot key expires at once and thousands of requests hit the DB simultaneously; mitigate with lock on miss or staggered TTL

nodes.label: Choose the realtime technique by actual need
nodes.norm_label: choose the realtime technique by actual need
nodes.rationale: WebSocket has higher overhead (reconnects, two-way state); SSE is simpler for listen-only; polling is fine when seconds of delay are acceptable; do not pick the fastest by default

nodes.label: Duplicate Charge from Retry
nodes.rationale: The first request succeeded but the response was lost, so a naive retry charges the customer twice.

nodes.label: Idempotency Key
nodes.rationale: Client-generated key tied to one intent and sent on every retry; the server checks it atomically and returns the stored result instead of repeating work. Needs a TTL and an atomic check-then-write to avoid races.

nodes.label: Naturally Idempotent Design
nodes.rationale: Make operations idempotent by design: use set-to-value instead of increment, and database unique constraints on client-supplied IDs.

nodes.label: CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type)
nodes.rationale: Data structures designed to merge automatically with no conflicts, e.g. a counter whose final value is the same regardless of merge order.

nodes.label: Last-Write-Wins
nodes.rationale: Simplest conflict resolution but can lose data if the wrong write wins.

nodes.label: Supporting multiple API versions
nodes.rationale: mobile apps update at different times so old versions stay in use for months; removing the old API immediately breaks users who did nothing wrong, so the server must support several versions before retiring old ones

nodes.label: Validate on both client and server
nodes.norm_label: validate on both client and server
nodes.rationale: client validation is for UX (fast, no round-trip); server validation is for security because requests can bypass the app (e.g. curl); treat every request as coming from an untrusted stranger

nodes.label: Anycast (root servers and 8.8.8.8)
nodes.rationale: only 13 root server IPs but each IP is announced from hundreds of machines worldwide; BGP routing sends a query to the nearest one, so no central load balancer is needed

nodes.label: HTTP lifecycle (7 steps from DNS to render)
nodes.norm_label: http lifecycle (7 steps from dns to render)

nodes.label: At-Least-Once Delivery
nodes.rationale: If a consumer disappears before ACK the message is redelivered, so work may run twice; handlers should be idempotent (set status = paid, not add money).

nodes.label: State Checkpoint
nodes.rationale: Periodic snapshot of processing state plus atomic offset commit lets a crashed worker recover accurately.

nodes.label: Exactly-Once Semantics
nodes.rationale: Means the result equals processing once, not that the network never duplicates. Matters more than for REST because stateful aggregation accumulates error from duplicates over time.

nodes.label: Circuit Breaker States (Closed, Open, Half-Open)
nodes.rationale: Closed passes traffic and counts failures; Open rejects immediately; Half-Open lets one trial request through to decide whether to close or reopen.

nodes.label: Thread Pool Exhaustion
nodes.rationale: Requests waiting on a dead downstream until timeout consume all threads, taking the calling service down too.

nodes.label: Jitter
nodes.rationale: Random offset on retry timing so many clients do not retry in lockstep.

nodes.label: Retry
nodes.rationale: Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 503), never definite failures like 400 or 401.

nodes.label: Retry Amplification
nodes.rationale: With 3 retries at every layer of a call chain the load on the failing leaf multiplies (3, 9, 27 requests), worsening the outage.

nodes.label: Thundering Herd
nodes.rationale: Many clients retrying simultaneously overload a recovering system again.

nodes.label: HTTP Method Idempotency (GET/PUT/DELETE vs POST)
nodes.rationale: GET, PUT and usually DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, so it needs added protection.

nodes.label: Idempotency
nodes.rationale: Repeating an operation leaves the same final result; essential because retries and at-least-once delivery cause duplicates.

nodes.label: Bulkhead Pattern
nodes.rationale: Give each downstream its own thread or connection pool quota so one slow dependency cannot starve calls to others; complements the circuit breaker.

nodes.label: Circuit Breaker
nodes.rationale: Fail fast instead of waiting on a failing downstream, so callers do not exhaust threads and the failure does not cascade.

nodes.label: Exponential Backoff
nodes.rationale: Double the wait after each failure (1, 2, 4, 8s) with a cap and a max attempt count so the server can recover instead of being hammered.

nodes.label: Retry Budget
nodes.rationale: Cap the fraction of traffic allowed to be retries (e.g. 10%) and retry only at the edge layer to prevent amplification.

nodes.rationale: no backend and no account; progress is kept only in the browser localStorage

nodes.label: Analogy-first teaching approach
nodes.rationale: explain with a concrete everyday analogy before introducing the technical term; diagrams and interactive demos accompany nearly every topic

nodes.label: Paxos
nodes.rationale: Older theoretically correct consensus algorithm but so complex that engineers interpret it differently in practice; still used in legacy systems like Google Chubby.

nodes.label: Raft
nodes.rationale: Consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos by separating leader election, log replication and safety; used by etcd, Consul, CockroachDB.

nodes.label: Split-Brain
nodes.rationale: Two or more nodes believe they are Primary and accept writes concurrently, producing conflicting data that is very hard to repair.

nodes.label: Term (Election Round Number)
nodes.rationale: Term increments each election so a returning old Primary sees a higher term and steps down to follower instead of fighting for leadership.

nodes.label: Client-Side Discovery
nodes.rationale: Each client keeps a copy of the instance list and load-balances itself, lowering registry load but making clients smarter.

nodes.label: DNS-Based Discovery
nodes.rationale: Stable DNS name per service resolves to healthy instance IPs so clients never talk to a registry API directly.

nodes.label: Self-Registration
nodes.rationale: Instance contains code to register itself and heartbeat; straightforward but every service embeds registry logic.

nodes.label: Server-Side Discovery
nodes.rationale: As described: the gateway consults the registry on every call; simpler for clients but the registry takes more load.

nodes.label: Service Discovery
nodes.rationale: Instance IPs change constantly as services scale, so hardcoding is impossible; a central registry acts like an always-updated phone book. Described as a load balancer for internal services with a changing instance count.

nodes.label: Service Registry
nodes.rationale: Instances register themselves, send heartbeats, and are removed automatically when heartbeats stop.

nodes.label: Third-Party Registration
nodes.rationale: An orchestrator observes instances being born or dying and registers them on their behalf, reducing coupling between services and the registry.

nodes.label: Leader Election
nodes.rationale: When the Primary dies suddenly, replicas must pick a new Primary without a central coordinator; unsafe self-appointment causes split-brain, so election needs a majority rule.

nodes.label: Raft Log Replication
nodes.rationale: Leader writes each command to its own log, sends it to followers, and commits only after a majority confirm; a stricter form of synchronous replication.

nodes.label: Majority Quorum Vote
nodes.rationale: A candidate needs more than half the votes; mathematically only one candidate can hold a majority in the same round, so split-brain is prevented. Odd node counts (3 or 5) are preferred because even counts add no extra fault tolerance (4 nodes need 3 votes, same as 5).

nodes.label: DNS-based load distribution
nodes.rationale: simple way to spread users over several addresses but much coarser than a real load balancer since nothing checks whether a host is still alive

nodes.label: HTTP is a stateless protocol
nodes.rationale: each request is independent so the server does not remember earlier calls; identity must be attached every time (cookie/token)

nodes.label: Autoscaling: CPU-based vs queue-depth-based
nodes.rationale: CPU-based is simple but late for I/O-bound work; queue depth reflects the real load of async workloads better

nodes.label: Direct Server Return (DSR)
nodes.rationale: responses bypass the LB because outbound data (e.g. video) is much heavier than inbound requests; otherwise LB bandwidth becomes the bottleneck

nodes.label: Load balancer as a new single point of failure
nodes.norm_label: load balancer as a new single point of failure
nodes.rationale: every fix for a single point carrying all load tends to create a new single point; the next question is how to make that new point non-single

nodes.label: Round Robin
nodes.rationale: simple and fair when requests cost about the same; a slot gets busier if it keeps receiving heavy requests despite equal request counts

nodes.label: Weighted Round Robin / Weighted Least Connections
nodes.norm_label: weighted round robin / weighted least connections

nodes.label: External Session Store (Redis)
nodes.rationale: move session data where every server can reach it; Redis is fast and has built-in TTL

nodes.label: JWT (JSON Web Token)
nodes.rationale: state lives in the token held by the client and the server only signs and verifies it, so any server can verify without asking Redis; trade-off is that revoking before expiry is hard

nodes.label: Short-lived JWT + refresh token
nodes.rationale: since JWT is hard to revoke, set a short TTL (e.g. 15 minutes) and pair with refresh tokens

nodes.label: Stateful server
nodes.rationale: session in server memory, uploaded files on one disk or an in-process cache make a server stateful by accident

nodes.label: Sticky session
nodes.rationale: binds a user to one server via cookie; if it dies the state is lost, the LB cannot choose freely, and heavy users overload one machine

nodes.label: Hybrid: scale up to a cost-effective size, then scale out
nodes.norm_label: hybrid: scale up to a cost-effective size, then scale out
nodes.rationale: production systems scale up until it stops being worth it (mid-size machines) and then repeat that size by scaling out

nodes.label: Stateless is the foundation of horizontal scaling
nodes.norm_label: stateless is the foundation of horizontal scaling
nodes.rationale: if every server holds its own state, adding servers does not help because users must return to the same one; shared access to the same data is what makes more machines meaningful

nodes.label: Schema Registry
nodes.rationale: Central store of every event schema version that auto-checks compatibility before a new schema may be published.

nodes.label: Saga Orchestration
nodes.rationale: A central Saga Orchestrator knows the steps and compensations; easier to debug but must itself be fault tolerant.

nodes.label: Active-Active
nodes.rationale: All replicas serve traffic at once; efficient and no switchover, but requires stateless design and handling concurrent writes.

nodes.label: Active-Passive
nodes.rationale: Standby idles until the primary fails; simple but wastes standby resources.

nodes.label: Failover
nodes.rationale: A health checker detects a dead primary and switches traffic to a standby via DNS or load balancer; a standby never tested may be broken when needed.

nodes.label: Big Bang Deployment
nodes.rationale: Replace everything at once: lowest cost, but 100% of users hit a bug immediately and rollback needs downtime.

nodes.label: Blue-Green Deployment
nodes.rationale: Two identical environments with one traffic switch; very fast rollback but double the resources.

nodes.label: Deployment Strategies
nodes.rationale: Failures caused by our own new releases are the most dangerous, so choose a rollout method that limits blast radius and allows fast rollback.

nodes.label: Rolling Deployment
nodes.rationale: Replace instances gradually with no downtime; v1 and v2 run together so APIs and schemas must be backward compatible.

nodes.label: Backward/Forward-Compatible Event Schema Evolution
nodes.rationale: Subscribers deploy at different times, so only add optional fields, never remove or rename in use fields; deprecate first and delete once nobody depends on them.

nodes.label: Chaos Engineering
nodes.rationale: Deliberately inject failures in a controlled setting (e.g. Chaos Monkey) to prove failover works before a real outage picks its own worst time.

nodes.label: GraphQL
nodes.rationale: Client specifies the exact fields it needs in one query, fixing over/under-fetching and suiting diverse clients, at the cost of resolver complexity and harder HTTP caching.

nodes.label: gRPC
nodes.rationale: Schema-first binary protocol with built-in streaming; faster and best for internal service-to-service traffic where both sides share the schema.

nodes.label: Over-fetching and Under-fetching
nodes.rationale: Server-fixed response shapes in REST and gRPC return too much data or force multiple calls.

nodes.label: REST
nodes.rationale: HTTP verbs with human-readable JSON and broad tooling support; best for public and third-party APIs.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.rationale: Single entry point so clients need not know each microservice; routes by content, unlike a plain load balancer. It becomes a single point of failure, so run more than one.

nodes.label: Gateway Responsibilities (routing, central auth, rate limit, aggregation, logging)
nodes.norm_label: gateway responsibilities (routing, central auth, rate limit, aggregation, logging)
nodes.rationale: Centralizing cross-cutting concerns avoids duplicating auth, rate limiting and logging in every service.

nodes.label: Boundary Spike (Fixed Window Flaw)
nodes.rationale: With a fixed 100/sec window a client can send 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next, giving 200 within one real second.

nodes.label: Rate Limiting
nodes.rationale: Caps requests per time window so one client cannot exhaust the system; placed at the gateway or load balancer so rejected traffic never reaches the database.

nodes.label: BFF (Backend For Frontend)
nodes.rationale: A separate gateway per client type (mobile, web) so each frontend team owns its own aggregation logic and the shared gateway does not become an organizational bottleneck.

nodes.label: Sliding Window Counter
nodes.rationale: Weights the previous window by elapsed fraction of the current one for a smooth, more accurate count at the cost of slightly more complex logic; suited to billing APIs.

nodes.label: Token Bucket
nodes.rationale: Tokens refill at a fixed rate up to a cap; each request spends one, allowing controlled bursts and reducing boundary spikes.

nodes.label: JourneyDiagram (animation demo component)
nodes.rationale: used in only 9 topics on purpose: animation suits flows with a real sequence of steps, not every topic has a journey to tell

nodes.label: "หัวข้อเงียบ" (13 topics without interactive demo)
nodes.norm_label: "หัวขอเงียบ" (13 topics without interactive demo)
nodes.rationale: content-complete (diagram, marks, ADR present) but nothing to click, unlike topics with step-through demos

nodes.label: Choosing TCP vs UDP: does losing a packet matter?
nodes.norm_label: choosing tcp vs udp: does losing a packet matter?
nodes.rationale: TCP for money transfer, web and files where loss is unacceptable; UDP for video calls, games and DNS where one lost frame goes unnoticed

nodes.label: Why DNS uses UDP
nodes.rationale: a query/response is one short round trip so registered-mail style checking would cost more than the data; a lost packet just means asking again

nodes.label: Consistent Hashing
nodes.rationale: hash a user ID to a server so the same user returns to the same machine; the same principle decides which node stores a key in caching and sharding

nodes.label: Power of Two Choices (P2C)
nodes.rationale: sample two servers and send to the one with fewer connections; close to Least Connections without tracking every server state in real time

nodes.label: Virtual Nodes
nodes.rationale: with only 3-4 servers hash positions on the ring are uneven; giving each server many virtual points smooths the distribution (law of large numbers)

nodes.label: Asynchronous replication
nodes.rationale: fastest: acknowledge before replicas receive data; data is lost if the primary dies before shipping it

nodes.label: Synchronous replication
nodes.rationale: wait for at least one replica before acknowledging so no loss, but every write pays a network round trip (50-200ms across regions)

nodes.label: Directory-based sharding
nodes.rationale: a lookup table records which key lives on which shard so any key can be moved freely; costs an extra lookup hop and the directory itself must scale and tolerate failure

nodes.label: Hot shard
nodes.rationale: even key counts do not guarantee even traffic; monitor per-shard traffic and rebalance hot keys

nodes.label: Mod-N rehash moves almost every key
nodes.norm_label: mod-n rehash moves almost every key

nodes.label: Range-based sharding
nodes.rationale: simple but one shard can become overloaded when new keys cluster in one range (e.g. ever-increasing user ids)

nodes.label: Sharding key selection
nodes.rationale: pick a key most queries already filter by (e.g. user_id)

nodes.label: Sharding vs replication
nodes.rationale: replication copies the same data (read scale, fault tolerance) while sharding splits different data (storage and write scale); real systems use both

nodes.label: Two questions for choosing an algorithm
